kcet|Chemistry|2016|35||0|0.s:
Use VSEPR. Xenon has 8 valence electrons; six are used bonding to six fluorines, leaving one
lone pair.
Bonding pairs = 6, lone pairs = 1, so there are 7 electron domains.
Seven domains give a pentagonal bipyramidal arrangement, and placing the lone pair in one
position leaves the six fluorines in a distorted octahedron.
The lone pair is stereochemically active: it pushes the nearby Xe–F bonds away, so the F–Xe–F
angles are not the clean 90° of a regular octahedron.
Compare the series: XeF₂ has 3 lone pairs and is linear, XeF₄ has 2 and is square planar, XeF₆
has 1 and is distorted octahedral.
∴ distorted octahedral.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|36||0|0:
Count the donor atoms first: 2 Cl + 2 N from en + 2 N from NH₃ = 6, so the complex is octahedral.
The key constraint is that en is a bidentate ligand with a short backbone — it can only bridge
two *adjacent* (cis) positions, never trans.
Fix en across one cis edge. Four sites remain for 2 Cl and 2 NH₃, and these can be arranged as:
1. the two Cl trans to each other
2. the two Cl cis, with one Cl trans to a nitrogen of en
3. the two Cl cis, arranged the other way round
The trans-Cl form has a mirror plane and is achiral. The cis-Cl forms lack one, so one of them
exists as a non-superimposable pair of mirror images — a d and an l form.
Adding the optical pair to the geometrical ones gives four distinct isomers in all.
∴ four isomers.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|37||0|0:
Ligand strength in the spectrochemical series is not simply a matter of charge — if it were,
Cl⁻ would beat neutral CO, and it does not.
CO is a strong field ligand because it bonds in two ways at once (synergic bonding):
σ donation — the carbon lone pair goes into an empty metal d orbital.
π back-donation — a filled metal d orbital pushes electron density back into CO's empty π*
antibonding orbital. CO can accept this precisely because it has π bonds, and therefore π* orbitals.
That back-donation removes electron density from the metal's t₂g set, which widens the gap
between t₂g and e₉ and makes Δ₀ large.
Cl⁻ has no empty π* orbital to accept back-donation. It is a π *donor* instead, which pushes
the t₂g level up and shrinks Δ₀ — so it is a weak field ligand.
∴ because CO has π-bonds.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|38||0|0.s:
Paramagnetism rises with the number of unpaired electrons, μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM.
Write the configuration of each ion. For a transition metal cation the 4s electrons go first.
Mn²⁺ : Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s² ⇒ Mn²⁺ = 3d⁵ ⇒ five orbitals, one electron each, n = 5
Cu²⁺ : Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ ⇒ Cu²⁺ = 3d⁹ ⇒ n = 1
Sc²⁺ : Sc is [Ar]3d¹4s² ⇒ Sc²⁺ = 3d¹ ⇒ n = 1 (and Sc²⁺ is not a common ion)
Cu⁺ : 3d¹⁰ ⇒ n = 0, diamagnetic — and it is not bivalent anyway
d⁵ is the half-filled case and gives the maximum possible for the 3d series:
μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 = 5.92 BM
∴ Mn²⁺.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|39||0|0.s:
Identify A from the description: a brown compound of manganese. That is MnO₂, a dark brown solid.
Step 1 — MnO₂ with concentrated HCl is the laboratory preparation of chlorine:
MnO₂ + 4HCl ⇒ MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O
so B = Cl₂, a greenish-yellow gas.
Step 2 — chlorine with ammonia, and the amount matters.
With *excess ammonia*: 8NH₃ + 3Cl₂ ⇒ 6NH₄Cl + N₂
With *excess chlorine*: NH₃ + 3Cl₂ ⇒ NCl₃ + 3HCl
The question says the gas is taken in excess, so chlorine is in excess and the product is
nitrogen trichloride.
NCl₃ is a notoriously explosive oily yellow liquid, which matches 'explosive compound' ✓
∴ A = MnO₂, B = Cl₂, C = NCl₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|40||0|0.s:
Oxidation from +2 to +3 means removing a third electron, so compare the third ionisation energies.
Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ — exactly half filled, with one electron in each of the five d orbitals and all spins
parallel. This is an especially stable arrangement because of its symmetry and its large exchange energy.
Taking a further electron away destroys that half-filled stability, so the third ionisation energy
of manganese is abnormally high and Mn²⁺ resists oxidation.
Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ — one electron has had to pair up. Losing that paired electron actually *gives* the
stable 3d⁵ configuration, so it is easy, Fe's third ionisation energy is lower, and Fe²⁺ is readily
oxidised to Fe³⁺.
That is why Fe²⁺ salts darken in air while Mn²⁺ salts are stable.
(3) is wrong: 3d⁵ is half filled, not completely filled.
∴ because Mn²⁺ is stabilised by its high third ionisation energy.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|41||0|0:
The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by the size of the crystal field splitting Δ₀ they produce.
The usual ordering, weak field to strong field, runs:
I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < NO₂⁻ < CN⁻ < CO
Taking just the four asked about and keeping that order:
SCN⁻ < F⁻ < CN⁻ < CO
The reasoning behind the ends of the series: SCN⁻ bonded through sulphur is a large, polarisable,
π-donating ligand and splits weakly, while CN⁻ and CO are π acceptors whose back-bonding
widens Δ₀ the most.
Note the series is not a charge ordering — neutral CO outranks every anion here, which is why
it has to be learned as an experimental sequence.
∴ SCN⁻ < F⁻ < CN⁻ < CO.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|42||0|0.s:
Name the complex ion first, then the counter ion.
Ligands are cited alphabetically, ignoring the multiplying prefixes:
chlorido (Cl⁻), ethane-1,2-diamine (en), nitrito-O (ONO⁻).
en already contains numbers in its name, so the multiplying prefix must be bis, not di, and the
name is enclosed in brackets: bis(ethane-1,2-diamine).
The ambidentate ligand ONO⁻ is bonded through oxygen, shown by writing the donor atom first
in the formula; that linkage isomer is named nitrito-O. (Bonded through nitrogen it would be
written NO₂ and named nitrito-N, the old 'nitro'.)
Oxidation state: the complex ion is +1 because one Cl⁻ sits outside. Inside, en is neutral and
Cl⁻ and ONO⁻ are each −1, so x − 2 = +1 and x = +3.
The chloride outside is named last as the anion.
∴ chlorido bis(ethane-1,2-diamine) nitrito-O-cobalt(III) chloride.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|43||0|0.s:
Work backwards from the product.
B + HNO₂ gives CH₃CH₂OH. Nitrous acid converts an aliphatic **primary amine** into an alcohol,
through an unstable diazonium salt that loses N₂ at once:
CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HNO₂ ⇒ CH₃CH₂OH + N₂ + H₂O
So B = CH₃CH₂NH₂, ethylamine.
Now A on reduction gives ethylamine. A nitrile reduces to a primary amine with the same
number of carbons plus the nitrile carbon:
CH₃CN + 4[H] ⇒ CH₃CH₂NH₂
So A = CH₃CN, ethane nitrile (acetonitrile).
Check the carbon count: CH₃CN has 2 carbons, and so does ethylamine ✓ Propane nitrile would
have given propylamine, one carbon too many.
∴ A is ethane nitrile.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|44||0|0.s:
Work backwards from the end.
C on catalytic reduction gives N-methylbenzenamine, C₆H₅NHCH₃ — a secondary amine with one
methyl on the nitrogen. Reducing an isocyanide, R–NC, gives exactly that: R–NH–CH₃.
So C = C₆H₅NC, phenyl isocyanide.
C was made from B with trichloromethane and caustic potash. That is the carbylamine reaction,
and it works only on **primary amines**:
C₆H₅NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH ⇒ C₆H₅NC + 3KCl + 3H₂O
So B = C₆H₅NH₂, aniline.
B came from reducing A, and the standard route to aniline is the reduction of nitrobenzene:
C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] ⇒ C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O
∴ A is nitrobenzene.
